text: You get a binary string s, and two integers, min jump and max jump. You start at index zero, and the first character is always a zero. From index i, you can jump to index j, as long as j is at least i plus min jump, at most i plus max jump, not past the end of the string, and the character at j is a zero. Return true if you can reach the last index.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — a one is a wall. I can never land on it. A zero is a spot I can land on. And every jump is at least min jump and at most max jump to the right. I never move left. Is that right?

Good. Then I want to flip the question around. Instead of asking where can I go from i, I'll ask: who can jump into i? A cell j can reach i only if j sits in the range from i minus max jump up to i minus min jump. So index i is reachable when its character is a zero, and at least one reachable cell sits in that range. That range is the whole problem. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Length is from two up to ten to the fifth. Each character is a zero or a one. And min jump is at least one, at most max jump, and max jump is less than the length.

Okay. So max jump can be almost as big as n. That matters for the cost — I'll come back to it. Let me run through the example. The string is zero one one zero one zero, min jump two, max jump three. From index zero, I can jump to two or three. Index two is a wall, index three is open. From three, I can jump to five. Index five is the last one, and it's a zero. So the path is zero, to three, to five, and the answer is true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to keep a dp array, and for each index i, scan the whole range, from i minus max jump up to i minus min jump, to look for one true cell. That's correct, but it costs n times the window width. With all zeros, n at ten to the fifth, min jump one, max jump ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, the naive scan took about one point eight seconds when I measured it. That's way too slow. This problem reminds me of a sliding window. Here's why. When i moves right by one, the range also moves right by one. Exactly one cell comes in on the right — the one at i minus min jump. Exactly one cell drops off on the left — the one at i minus max jump minus one. So I don't need to rescan. I just update a running number. I'll go with the sliding-window DP. It's one pass, and the window update is constant time per step.

Here's the plan. I keep a dp array, where dp of i means: can I stand on index i? The start is true. And I keep a counter, cnt, which is the number of true dp values inside the window — the cells that could jump into i. Then for each i from min jump to the end: if the cell at i minus min jump is true, the counter goes up by one — that cell just entered the window. If the cell at i minus max jump minus one exists and is true, the counter goes down by one — that cell just left. Then dp of i is true when the counter is above zero and the character at i is a zero. At the end I return the last dp value. So here I'm using cnt to keep track of how many reachable cells are inside the window right now. The invariant is simple: after the two updates, cnt is exactly the number of true dp values in the window. If it's above zero, someone can jump into i. One thing worth flagging — it has to be a count, not a yes-or-no flag. Let me walk through that. The window can hold more than one reachable cell. When one of them leaves, a flag would flip to false, even if another reachable cell is still inside. A count just goes down by one and stays correct. The tricky part is that a flag version passes both examples. It still fails on the string zero zero zero with jumps one and one: it says false, but the right answer is true. There's a trade-off here. I could also do breadth-first search with a farthest pointer, so each index gets visited once. It's also linear. I like the DP because the window count is easy to prove and easy to dry-run. The cost is a linear-size dp array. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up — I'll talk through it rather than read it line by line. I take the length n, make a dp array of n ints, all false, set the first one to true, and start the counter at zero. Then one loop, i from min jump up to n minus one. First the enter step: if dp at i minus min jump is true, the counter goes up. Then the leave step: if i minus max jump minus one is at least zero, and the dp there is true, the counter goes down. Then the decision: dp of i is true when the counter is above zero and the character at i is a zero. After the loop I return the last dp value. That matches the plan. The loop starts at min jump, because no index before that can be reached from zero — those cells just stay false. One thing worth flagging — the remove guard checks at least zero, not strictly above zero. With the strict version, the start cell never leaves the window, so it keeps helping cells it can't really reach. On the string zero one zero, with jumps one and one, that bug returns true, but the answer is false. So this guard is a correctness rule, not a small detail. Same idea for the zero check on the character at i. If I drop it, a wall can be marked reachable. The string zero one, with jumps one and one, would come back true, and it should be false.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. I'll use example one: the string zero one one zero one zero, min jump two, max jump three. Expected output is true. Enters is the cell two back, leaves is the cell four back, and cnt is the value after both updates. At i equals two, the start cell enters, so cnt is one — but index two is a wall, so its dp stays false. At i equals three, a false cell enters, cnt stays one, and index three is open, so dp of three becomes true. The key row is i equals four. Here the start cell slides out of the window, so cnt drops to zero. Index four is a wall anyway, but this is the moment the window really forgets old cells. Then at i equals five, dp of three comes in, cnt goes back to one, and index five is a zero. So the final dp is true, false, false, true, false, true, and we return true. That's the same zero, three, five path. Example two, the string zero one one zero one one one zero, with jumps two and three, returns false. Index three is the only reachable cell after the start. While it's inside the window, at i equals five and six, those cells are walls. At i equals seven, dp of three leaves, so cnt is zero and the last index stays false. Let's also test with corner cases. Two zeros with jumps one and one: true — smallest input, one jump. Zero then one: false — the last cell is a wall. Three zeros with jumps one and one: true — that's the case where the flag version says false. Zero one zero with jumps one and one: false — that's where the wrong guard says true. Four zeros with jumps fixed at two: false — no wall, but parity blocks it. And all zeros with n at ten to the fifth and a fixed jump of two: false, because the last index is odd. That four-zeros case is a nice one. There's no wall at all, but with a fixed jump of two I only land on even indices. So no long run of ones is not enough. A run of ones at least max jump long always blocks you, but with min jump two or more there are gaps too. The DP handles both for free.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is linear. Each index does one add check and one remove check, both constant time. The space complexity is linear, for the dp array. In the worst case for the naive scan — all zeros, min jump one, max jump ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, n at ten to the fifth — the window holds up to almost a hundred thousand reachable cells. The naive version took about one point eight seconds. This version took about a hundred and five microseconds, because the window size never shows up in the cost. Oh, one more thing — I return the last dp value, not whether the counter is above zero. The counter only says someone can jump into the last index. It ignores whether the last cell is a wall. The string zero one, with jumps one and one, shows it: the counter is above zero, which gives true, but the answer is false. And that bug also passes both examples, so it's easy to miss.
Good. Could you do it without the window count?

Two ways. First, breadth-first search with a farthest pointer. I pop a reachable index i and look at the range from i plus min jump to i plus max jump. But I keep a pointer to the farthest index I already checked, and I start from there. So every index is looked at once. On the same worst case it ran in about a hundred and eighteen microseconds, about the same as the DP. Second, a prefix-sum version. I keep a running count of how many dp values are true in the first k cells. Then, any reachable cell in the window, is just one subtraction of two prefix values. It's the same idea as the counter, written as a range sum. Also, a vector of bools works and is much smaller — about twelve and a half thousand bytes versus four hundred thousand for a vector of ints. But it was about three times slower in my run, around three hundred microseconds. So I kept the vector of ints.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You flipped the question to, who can jump into i, which turned a graph search into a window that slides one step at a time. You explained why the window needs a count, not a flag, and backed it with the three-zeros case — a bug that passes both examples. And you showed that the remove guard, the character check, and returning the last dp value are each correctness rules, with a small input that breaks each one. Good work.
